title: Teamwork & delegation
blurb: Delegating safely within scope and competence, supervision, handover, resolving disagreements and working as one team in an emergency.
question: Halfway through a busy list, the dentist asks you to take on a task you have only watched once. At the same time, the practice manager asks you to cover reception between patients. How do you decide whether to accept the task, and how do you respond to the extra workload?

teach.h: Why teamwork is a patient-safety issue
teach.body: GDC Standards Principle 6 says you must work with colleagues in a way that is in patients' best interests. Good teams share information, check each other's work and speak up early, so fewer mistakes reach the patient. Teams made up of people from different backgrounds bring different viewpoints and help patients from all communities feel understood. Poor teamwork shows up as rushed turnarounds, missed checks and patients hearing mixed messages.

Delegating means asking a colleague to carry out a task on your behalf. The GDC says you can only delegate to someone who is trained, competent and indemnified or insured for that task, and it must be within their scope of practice. There should be mutual agreement, the colleague should be encouraged to ask questions, and they must not be pressured into a task they don't feel trained or competent to do. The person who delegates keeps overall responsibility for the patient's care. The person who accepts is responsible for how well they carry the task out.

teach.h: A task is delegated to you

children.label: Accept
children.sub: Clarify what's needed; ask if unsure

teach.caption: If you feel you are not trained or competent, the GDC says you should not be pressured into accepting.

teach.text: Delegating a task does not hand over responsibility for the patient. The dentist who delegates keeps overall responsibility; you are accountable for your own part.

teach.body: Effective supervision means being present and able to step in, with clear limits agreed before the procedure starts. A student or trainee dental nurse should only do what they have been assessed as competent to do, under supervision. Their confidence alone is not enough. If you supervise someone, you share responsibility for making sure the patient stays safe.

letters.sub: Who the patient is and what's happening now
Relevant history and stage of treatment
Any concerns, e.g. anxiety or a medical alert
What still needs doing and by whom

teach.caption: When you hand over partway through a list, the key facts are the treatment stage, any concerns and what remains to be done.

teach.body: When patients get conflicting advice from different team members, they lose confidence and may follow the wrong instructions. Agree a shared approach based on practice policy. If a colleague does something that bothers you, raise it with them directly, calmly and in private first. If the problem is about the system, such as surgeries always running late, take it to a team meeting with suggestions. Regular meetings let the team share information, review incidents and agree changes.

steps.label: Team meeting
steps.sub: If it's a system or repeated issue

steps.label: Manager or policy
steps.sub: If it can't be resolved informally

teach.body: If you are asked to cover reception and chairside at once, or to work through your break on a packed list, don't just quietly agree or flatly refuse. Explain the risk to patient care and agree priorities with your manager. In a medical emergency, the team works best when one person leads and gives everyone a clear role, rather than several people giving instructions at once.

head: Role
Job
rows: Directs the team and allocates roles
Assesses ABCDE, starts CPR if needed
Brings oxygen, emergency drugs and AED
Records times, observations and drugs given
teach.caption: In a small team, one person may cover more than one role. Everyone must know their role before an emergency happens.

items: Delegate only to someone trained, competent and indemnified, within their scope, with mutual agreement.
The delegating dentist keeps overall responsibility; you are accountable for your own work.
Supervision: be present, able to intervene, with limits agreed; students do only what they're assessed competent for.
Handover: treatment stage, concerns, what remains (SBAR).
Raise issues with the colleague first; system problems go to team meetings; unsafe workload is discussed with the manager.
In an emergency, one leader allocates clear roles.

summary: You can now explain when delegation is appropriate and who stays responsible, decide whether to accept a task, supervise a trainee safely, give a structured handover, resolve disagreements in the right order, respond professionally to unsafe workload and work in a led team during an emergency.

A.q: A dentist asks you to take on a task during a busy list. What makes this delegation appropriate?
options: You are trained and competent to do it
The list is running behind schedule
You have watched it done once before
No other team member is free right now
A.why: You can only accept a delegated task that is within your scope and that you are trained, competent and indemnified to do.

whyNot.1: Time pressure is never a reason to delegate to someone who isn't competent.
whyNot.2: Watching once doesn't make you competent; competence needs training and assessment.
whyNot.3: Staff availability doesn't make a task safe to delegate.

A.q: You are handing over to a colleague partway through a list. What is most important to pass on?
options: How many patients you have seen so far
Which instruments you prefer for the procedure
The treatment stage, concerns and what's left
The name and time of the next patient only
A.why: A safe handover covers where treatment is up to, any concerns and what remains to be done.

whyNot.0: A patient count doesn't help your colleague care for the patient in the chair.
whyNot.1: Personal preferences don't keep the patient safe.
whyNot.3: The next patient's name alone misses the clinical details your colleague needs.

A.q: A patient collapses in the waiting room. Three team members rush over and start giving different instructions. What would best support an effective response?
options: Everyone acting on their own initiative to save time
One person leading and allocating clear roles
The most senior dentist doing every task
Waiting for the paramedics before acting
A.why: Emergencies are managed best when one leader directs the team and each person has a clear role.

whyNot.0: Acting independently causes confusion, gaps and duplication.
whyNot.2: One person can't do everything at once; tasks must be shared.
whyNot.3: The team must start basic life support and emergency care straight away.

B.q: A dentist delegates a task to you. Who keeps overall responsibility for the patient's care?
options: The dental nurse doing the task
The practice manager on duty
The patient's own GP
The dentist who delegated it
B.why: The person who delegates keeps overall responsibility for the patient, even though the task has been handed on.

whyNot.0: You are accountable for how you carry out the task, but overall responsibility stays with the delegating dentist.
whyNot.1: The practice manager runs the business; they aren't responsible for clinical care.
whyNot.2: The GP has no role in a dental task delegated within the practice.

B.q: You are supervising a student dental nurse who asks whether they can carry out a task alone. What should guide your answer?
options: How confident the student says they feel about it
What they've been assessed as competent to do
How busy the surgery is this session
Whether the patient seems calm and relaxed
B.why: Students should only do what they have been assessed as competent to do, and then under supervision.

whyNot.0: Self-reported confidence is not evidence of competence.
whyNot.2: Workload doesn't change what a student is safe to do.
whyNot.3: A calm patient doesn't make an untrained person competent.

B.q: After an extraction, the dentist and the nurse give the patient different post-operative instructions. What is the main risk?
options: The CQC will fine the practice on the spot
The extraction will have to be repeated
The patient may follow the wrong advice
The patient's NHS charge band will change
B.why: Conflicting advice confuses patients, damages their trust in the team and can lead to complications if they follow the wrong instructions.

whyNot.0: The CQC doesn't issue on-the-spot fines for mixed messages; the risk is to the patient.
whyNot.1: The procedure itself is done; the problem is the aftercare.
whyNot.3: Charge bands depend on the treatment provided, not on the advice given.

C.q: You are asked to cover reception and assist chairside at the same time during a fully booked list. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Agree, and skip chairside checks to save time
Refuse, and leave the surgery until it's sorted
Accept quietly, then complain to colleagues afterwards
Explain the risk; agree priorities with the manager
C.why: Unsafe workload should be raised professionally: explain the risk to patient care and agree priorities with the manager.

whyNot.0: Skipping checks puts patients at risk.
whyNot.1: Walking away leaves patients and colleagues without support.
whyNot.2: Complaining to colleagues doesn't solve the problem or protect patients.

C.q: A colleague keeps leaving you to clean the surgery alone at the end of the day. What is the best first step?
options: Raise it calmly and directly with the colleague
Report the colleague to the GDC for misconduct
Leave their share of the cleaning undone too
Mention it in the staff group chat so others know
C.why: Most team problems are best raised directly, calmly and privately with the colleague first.

whyNot.1: This is a workplace issue, not a fitness to practise matter; going to the regulator first is disproportionate.
whyNot.2: Leaving the surgery unclean puts infection control and patients at risk.
whyNot.3: Discussing a colleague in a group chat is unprofessional and won't resolve it.

C.q: Why should a dental practice hold regular team meetings?
options: To let the manager allocate annual leave fairly
To replace the need for written practice policies
To share updates, review incidents, agree changes
To discuss each patient's treatment plan in detail
C.why: Team meetings let everyone share information, learn from incidents and agree changes together.

whyNot.0: Leave can be arranged without a team meeting; that isn't their main purpose.
whyNot.1: Meetings support policies; they don't replace them.
whyNot.3: Individual treatment plans are for the clinician and patient, not team meetings.

reteach.title: Think of a pit crew
reteach.question: A racing pit crew changes four tyres in seconds without anyone getting hurt. What do they do that a dental team should copy?

blocks.h: Everyone knows their job and their limits
blocks.body: In a pit crew, nobody grabs a wheel gun they haven't been trained on. One person leads and signals. When a crew member hands over, they say exactly what's done and what isn't. A dental team works the same way: you only take on tasks you're trained and competent for, the dentist who delegates still owns the outcome, handovers are clear, and in an emergency one person leads.

steps.label: In scope?
steps.sub: Is a dental nurse allowed to do it?

blocks.text: "I've seen it done" is not the same as "I'm competent". Competence needs training and assessment.

explain.body: Delegate only within the colleague's scope, and only if they are trained, competent and indemnified. Both must agree and the colleague must not be pressured. The delegating dentist keeps overall responsibility for the patient.

test.q: Which is a requirement before a task can be delegated to a dental nurse?
options: The nurse has been qualified for over a year
The task is in scope and the nurse is competent
The patient has agreed in writing
The practice manager has approved it
test.why: Delegation must be within the colleague's scope, and they must be trained, competent and indemnified.

whyNot.0: Length of service doesn't prove competence for a specific task.
whyNot.2: Written patient consent to delegation isn't the requirement; the colleague's scope and competence are.
whyNot.3: Managers don't authorise clinical delegation; the delegating clinician must check scope and competence.

explain.body: A supervisor stays present and able to intervene, with limits agreed beforehand. Trainees work only within what they've been assessed as competent to do.

rows.label: Available by phone in another room
Student decides what they can do

test.q: What does effective supervision of a trainee during a procedure require?
options: Being present and able to intervene
Being reachable by phone if needed
Checking their work at the end of the day
Letting them decide their own limits
test.why: Supervision means being present and able to step in, with limits agreed beforehand.

whyNot.1: Being on the phone elsewhere doesn't allow you to intervene in time.
whyNot.2: Checking afterwards is too late to protect the patient.
whyNot.3: Limits must be agreed based on assessed competence, not the trainee's own judgement.

explain.body: When you hand over a patient or a list, use a structure so nothing is missed: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. The essentials are the treatment stage, any concerns and what remains.

steps.label: Background
steps.sub: LA given 10 min ago; on warfarin

steps.label: Recommendation
steps.sub: Haemostatic kit ready; post-op advice due

test.q: Which handover gives a colleague the information they need?
options: "Mrs K is in the chair; the dentist knows the rest"
"Everything's fine with her, nothing to report really"
"LA given, on warfarin, anxious; post-op advice due"
"Your next patient is booked in at half past ten"
test.why: It gives the treatment stage, the concerns and what is still to be done.

whyNot.0: It passes the responsibility on without any useful detail.
whyNot.1: It hides the concerns your colleague needs to know.
whyNot.3: It ignores the patient currently being treated.

explain.body: Raise issues with the colleague first; take system problems to team meetings; escalate to the manager if needed. Discuss unsafe workload with your manager. In emergencies, one leader allocates roles.

test.q: Your surgery regularly runs behind and turnarounds are rushed. What is the most constructive action?
options: Rush the decontamination to catch up
Complain about the dentist to patients
Ignore it, as it's not your responsibility
Raise it at a team meeting with suggestions
test.why: A repeated system problem is best raised at a team meeting with suggestions for improvement.

whyNot.0: Rushing decontamination puts patients at risk.
whyNot.1: Complaining to patients is unprofessional and damages trust.
whyNot.2: Everyone in the team shares responsibility for safe, smooth running.
